generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, your practice and work-based learning is usually assessed through a reflective account or log, not through the placement itself. Supervisors and tutors are guided by professional standards, such as those of the British Psychological Society. They look for evidence that you can reflect on your own practice: what a session revealed about how you work, how it connects to theory and ethics, and what you will change. The account is the thing that is marked.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students submit a reflective account of the same clinical placement.

Tom writes a clear, orderly account of what the placement involved: the service, the daily routine, the assessments he observed. It reads well and is accurate. But it is a description. It tells the assessor what happened and little about what Tom learned, so there is almost nothing to credit as reflection or insight.

Amara writes less about the routine and more about what it revealed. She describes one assessment where she misread a client's cue, reflects on her part in it, links it to a professional guideline on rapport she had studied, and sets out what she now does differently and why. The account shows evidenced insight into her own practice. That is what the criteria reward.

Both students did the same placement and wrote to the same length. Only Amara articulated the learning, which is what is actually assessed.
generatedProse.summary: Practice- and work-based learning in psychology is assessed through reflection because every setting differs: what is marked is the learning you articulate, not the placement itself. A strong reflective account moves beyond description to evidenced insight, honest reflection, a link to theory or professional standards, and a specific change you will make. You can now explain how this learning is assessed, articulate your own learning, and judge an account against what assessors look for. You can turn any psychological experience into learning you can show.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's account stronger than Tom's?

items.text: It showed evidenced insight into her own learning, not just a description of events.
It described the placement in more detail.
It was written more clearly and was better organised.
It was longer than Tom's account.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara's account showed evidenced insight into her own learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara's account showed beyond a description of events.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's account was stronger because it showed evidenced insight into her learning. Detail, clarity and length were not the difference.
